source: MAFF Department of Agricultural Extension (នាយកដ្ឋានផ្សព្វផ្សាយកសិកម្ម) - "ដំណាំក្រូចពោធិសាត់" (Pursat Orange Cultivation Guide), 2016, 26pp
text:
Air-layering (marcotting) is done on a healthy, pest-free branch, ideally about the thickness of a finger. A ring of bark is removed around the branch to interrupt the flow of nutrients, which encourages the plant to form roots at that point. The wound is then wrapped with a moist rooting medium (traditionally coconut husk soaked and packed around the cut) and covered tightly with plastic sheeting, tied securely at both ends with wire or string so moisture is retained.

After roughly 2 to 3 months, roots should have filled the wrapped medium and be visible through the plastic. At that point the rooted branch is cut away below the new root ball and moved into a nursery pot to hold before it is planted out into the field.

Marcotted trees can begin bearing fruit sooner than seedling trees, but because they are grown from a cutting rather than a taproot, their root systems tend to be shallower. This makes them somewhat less drought-tolerant and generally shorter-lived in production than grafted trees, so farmers relying on marcots should plan on staking young trees for extra support and paying closer attention to watering during dry periods.
